source: Gugerty & Olson (1986) Debugging by skilled and novice programmers (CHI 86, pp.171-174)
finding: Two experiments compared expert and novice debuggers on programs given to them and run on a microcomputer. Programs were in LOGO in Experiment 1 and Pascal in Experiment 2.
numbers: 2 experiments; LOGO (Exp 1), Pascal (Exp 2). Subject counts not in the abstract I read.
limits: Only the abstract was read (via Crossref metadata). The full paper text was blocked (ACM 403, Academia 403).
agent_relevance: Sets the paradigm: the same bug-finding task on simple provided programs, expert vs novice.

source: Gugerty & Olson (1986) Debugging by skilled and novice programmers (CHI 86, pp.171-174)
finding: Experts debugged faster and more accurately. The reason given: they made high-quality hypotheses after studying the code less than novices did.
numbers: Speed and accuracy advantage for experts in both experiments (exact times and percentages not available to me).
quote: Experts debugged more quickly and accurately, largely because they generated high quality hypotheses on the basis of less study of the code than novices.
limits: Abstract only. Direction is certain; magnitudes are not.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis quality matters more than reading volume. The agent should reach a first hypothesis early, then test it, not read everything first.

source: Gugerty & Olson (1986) Debugging by skilled and novice programmers (CHI 86, pp.171-174)
finding: Novices often added new bugs to the program while trying to find the original one.
numbers: Described as 'frequently'; no count in the abstract.
quote: Further, novices frequently added bugs to the program during the course of trying to find the original one.
limits: Abstract only. Programs were simple. Bug-adding rate per edit unknown to me.
agent_relevance: Direct support for 'limit edits per round' and 'keep best-so-far': each edit by a weak hypothesiser can add a bug, so keep a verified copy and roll back.

source: Gugerty & Olson (1986) Debugging by skilled and novice programmers (CHI 86, pp.171-174)
finding: The authors' own conclusion: for these simple programs, experts' edge came mainly from better program comprehension, not from a different debugging procedure.
numbers: Conclusion stated for 'at least these simple programs'.
quote: At least for these simple programs, experts superior debugging performance seemed to be due primarily to their superior ability to comprehend the program.
limits: Authors hedge to simple programs. May not hold for large systems with hard bugs.
agent_relevance: Comprehension (a model of what the program should do) comes before edits. Maps to building a spec/restatement state before repair.

source: Gugerty & Olson (1986) Debugging by skilled and novice programmers (CHI 86, pp.171-174)
finding: The reference list of the CHI paper (as deposited in Crossref) has only 4 entries. Two are Jeffries conference papers: 'Computer program debugging by experts' (Psychonomic Society, 1981) and 'A comparison of the debugging behavior of expert and novice programmers' (AERA, 1982).
numbers: reference-count 4; is-referenced-by-count 15 in Crossref (low; most citers cite without DOI).
limits: Crossref lists may be incomplete. Backward citation: Jeffries 1981/1982 are the direct forerunners, both unpublished talks.
agent_relevance: Shows how thin the original base is: a 4-page paper on small programs, now cited as a general law.

source: Gugerty & Olson (1986), as summarised by secondary search results
finding: Secondary summaries (seen only as search snippets) say the first group was eighteen experts and six novices who debugged three programs, and that only one error was seeded in each program.
numbers: 18 experts, 6 novices, 3 programs, 1 seeded bug (UNVERIFIED snippet).
limits: Not opened: the page returned a bot-check; numbers come from a search snippet and must be checked against the full paper.
agent_relevance: If true, the novice group is tiny (6) and the bug was single. Treat novice-added-bug rates as weak evidence.

source: Kinnunen (2007) MSc thesis, Univ. of Eastern Finland, on eye-gaze and debugging strategies in Jeliot
finding: Describes the Gugerty & Olson strategy model: read the program description and code, form a hypothesis about the bug and the program's purpose, test it by editing, running or checking the description, and if no bug is found, go back to the description or code.
numbers: Cycle: introduction -> hypothesis -> test (modify / execute / description) -> return to introduction.
quote: In Gugerty & Olson study (1986), novice and expert programmers did not act any different but novices needed more time to do the same as the experts.
limits: Secondary description, not the paper; Figure 1 of the thesis redraws their model.
agent_relevance: This cycle is almost exactly an agent loop: read, hypothesise, test with a check, return on failure. Gives a human template for S-states.

source: Kinnunen (2007) MSc thesis
finding: The thesis reports that novices rarely found the bug on the first try and added new bugs while testing hypotheses. It also says experts and novices followed the same cycle, but novices took longer.
numbers: No numbers given.
limits: Tension: the paper's abstract stresses expert hypothesis quality, the thesis stresses same process but slower. A secondary reading; I could not check which matches the paper body.
agent_relevance: Suggests the gap is in the quality of each cycle, not the shape of the loop. So scaffold shape alone is not enough; the quality of the hypothesis slot matters.

source: Spoerer & Michaeli (2025) Investigating Debugging Processes: A Scoping Review (Koli Calling 25)
finding: Scoping review of 36 papers on students' debugging processes. Most used qualitative, inductive analysis of screen recordings. Most assessed either strategies or performance, rarely both. Few deductive studies of the whole process.
numbers: 36 papers.
limits: Covers student studies; Gugerty & Olson (1986) did not turn up by text search in the parts I extracted.
agent_relevance: Evidence base on novice debugging is mostly qualitative. Do not expect effect sizes to port to an agent.

source: Spoerer & Michaeli (2025) scoping review
finding: The review says McCauley et al. (2008) summarise debugging research to 2008, including expert-novice differences, and conclude debugging must be taught explicitly because it is not learned on the go with programming.
numbers: Cites Gould (1975) as an early ideal-typical expert process model, and Gilmore (1991) for a comprehension-centred model.
limits: Summary of another review, not primary.
agent_relevance: Backward lineage: Gould 1975 -> Jeffries 1981/82 -> Vessey 1985 -> Gugerty & Olson 1986 -> Katz & Anderson 1987 -> McCauley 2008.

source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs: a process analysis (Int J Man-Machine Studies)
finding: Crossref confirms the paper (Nov 1985, cited by 294). Only title and metadata were read, no abstract. The title says it analyses the process of expert debugging.
numbers: is-referenced-by-count 294.
limits: Metadata only; I did not read the findings.
agent_relevance: Lineage only. Another subfield row (Vessey strategy diagrams) holds its content.

source: Katz & Anderson (1987) Debugging: an analysis of bug-location strategies (Human-Computer Interaction 3(4))
finding: Crossref confirms the main follow-up on bug-location strategies (Dec 1987, cited by 143). Only metadata read.
numbers: is-referenced-by-count 143.
limits: Metadata only. An earlier search summary mentioned a Gugerty & Olson 1987 HCI paper; I found no such paper, and HCI 3(4) holds this Katz & Anderson paper, so that claim looks like a confusion.
agent_relevance: Forward lineage; the content belongs to the Angle B agents.

source: McCauley et al. (2008) Debugging: a review of the literature from an educational perspective (Computer Science Education 18(2))
finding: Crossref confirms the standard review (Jun 2008, cited by 227). Full text not obtained, so I cannot give its exact words about Gugerty & Olson.
numbers: is-referenced-by-count 227.
limits: Metadata only.
agent_relevance: Main route by which G&O reached later education research.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation? (ICLR 2024)
finding: Self-repair (the model debugs its own code) gives modest, uneven gains once the cost of repair is counted, and sometimes none. The bottleneck is the model's feedback on its own code.
numbers: With equal budget, GPT-4 on APPS: 10 samples then 1 repair each beat pass@20 by 1.05x; 2 samples then 10 repairs each fell below pass@22 (0.97x).
limits: Python tasks (HumanEval, APPS); Code Llama, GPT-3.5, GPT-4.
agent_relevance: LLM analogue of the novice finding: weak hypotheses make repair rounds worth less than fresh samples. Spend budget on diverse starts, not long repair chains.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet?
finding: Replacing GPT-4's own feedback with feedback written by human programmers raised the repair success rate of GPT-4.
numbers: Overall 33.30% -> 52.60% (1.58x). Introductory 42.64% -> 62.21%; interview 19.33% -> 45.67%; competition 3.67% -> 14.67%. 16 participants wrote 2 feedbacks each for 40 failing programs; 25 repairs sampled per feedback.
limits: Small study; humans spent about 1 hour; paid per survey. Gap grows with problem difficulty.
agent_relevance: Matches the expert-versus-novice story: the better hypothesis (feedback) drives the repair, not the editing. Hypothesis quality is the lever.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet?
finding: A stronger model supplying the feedback to a weaker model's repair beat both i.i.d. sampling and self-repair at all budgets tested.
numbers: Code Llama with GPT-3.5/GPT-4 feedback on HumanEval; GPT-3.5 with GPT-4 feedback on APPS (per-budget numbers not recorded).
limits: Needs a second, stronger model; correlated errors not tested here.
agent_relevance: Supports a separate diagnose slot, ideally with a different or stronger source, over letting the same text self-diagnose.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR 2024)
finding: Without oracle labels, asking the model to review and revise its own reasoning lowers accuracy on all benchmarks tested. With oracle labels, accuracy rises.
limits: Reasoning tasks, not code with tests. Oracle versions use the label to stop, which is not real self-correction. Table columns reconstructed from extracted text.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as novices adding bugs: edits without real evidence make things worse. Supports G2 (revise only from real output).

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Oracle-label self-correction gives big gains, but the authors say it is not a fair test because the answer is already known.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 -> 84.3; CSQA 75.8 -> 89.7; HotpotQA 26.0 -> 29.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 97.5; CSQA 82.0 -> 85.5; HotpotQA 49.0 -> 59.0 (as read from the extracted table).
limits: Table columns were reconstructed from extracted text; check against the PDF before quoting.
agent_relevance: A real check (tests, execution) acts like the oracle. So gate every edit on a check result.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: On GSM8K GPT-3.5 kept its first answer 74.7% of the time over two self-correction rounds. Among changes, it turned right answers into wrong ones more often than the reverse.
numbers: 74.7% unchanged on GSM8K (GPT-3.5).
limits: Direction for GPT-4 is better but still not a gain.
agent_relevance: Each extra edit round has a cost: keep best-so-far and revert unless a check says better.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location (Findings ACL 2024)
finding: Models are bad at finding the mistake but fairly good at fixing it once told where it is. Mistake finding is the weak step.
numbers: Best result: GPT-4 overall mistake-finding accuracy 52.87 with direct step-level prompting (other prompts 39.80 and 43.40 for GPT-4). GPT-3.5-Turbo low in some tasks (e.g. 10.10 and 19.00).
limits: BIG-Bench Mistake dataset, 5 reasoning tasks; not code debugging.
agent_relevance: Strong parallel to Gugerty & Olson: locating and hypothesising is the hard part; repair is easy given a location. Let code locate failures (G2).

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey
finding: The survey finds no prior work showing successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs, except on tasks exceptionally suited to it. Self-correction works when reliable external feedback exists, and large-scale fine-tuning also enables it.
numbers: Three conclusions: (1) no success with prompted-LLM feedback outside special tasks; (2) works with reliable external feedback; (3) works with large-scale fine-tuning.
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs, except for studies in tasks that are exceptionally suited
limits: Survey; depends on how papers define self-correction.
agent_relevance: Backs the design: use real execution output as the feedback source.

source: Adnan & Kuhn (2025) The Debugging Decay Index (arXiv 2506.18403)
finding: Iterative LLM debugging effectiveness falls on a fitted exponential curve. Most models lose 60-80% of debugging capability within 2-3 attempts.
numbers: HumanEval; six models; GPT-3.5-turbo reaches the 80% threshold at attempts 2-3; codestral:22b decay rate 0.375 and deepseek-coder:6.7b 0.330, giving windows of 5-7 attempts. Earlier work cited: 15 more attempts added only 2.4%.
limits: Preprint; effectiveness is normalised; mostly small open models.
agent_relevance: Directly the limit-edits-per-round rule: cap debugging rounds near 2-3 and then restart.

source: Adnan & Kuhn (2025) The Debugging Decay Index
finding: A fresh start (clear the conversation history) at the computed decay point beat plain continuous debugging at the same budget.
numbers: llama3.1:8b 72.56% -> 82.82% (best gain); deepseek-coder-v2:16b 84.1% -> 92.1%; Mistral-Instruct 54.3% -> 62.8%/57.3% at two thresholds. Token use similar or lower (deepseek-coder-v2 108,289 tokens baseline, lower with fresh starts).
limits: Preprint, one benchmark (HumanEval).
agent_relevance: Combine with keep-best-so-far: after 2-3 failed edits, restart from the best version with clean context.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering (NeurIPS 2024)
finding: A linter guard that rejects an edit if it introduces a syntax error raised resolve rate. A common failure is an agent introducing a syntax error and then editing the same snippet again and again.
numbers: Ablation: edit with linting 18.0%, edit without linting 15.0% (-3.0), no edit command 10.3% (-7.7). File viewer 30 lines 14.3%, 100 lines 18.0%, whole file 12.7%.
limits: Ablation on a SWE-bench subset with GPT-4 Turbo; small sample.
agent_relevance: The agent equivalent of novices adding bugs. Reject or roll back an edit that breaks a cheap check before it lands.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent
finding: Failed edits cluster and recovery gets harder with each one. 51.7% of trajectories had at least one failed edit.
numbers: Of 2,294 instances, 1,185 (51.7%) had 1+ failed edit, median 3, max 33. Recovery: 90.5% eventually succeed from any attempt, 57.2% after one failed edit. Resolved instances: 113 of 286 (31.5%) had a failed edit.
limits: GPT-4 Turbo trajectories on full SWE-bench; the paper also says agents succeed quickly and fail slowly.
agent_relevance: Strong numeric case for capping edits per round: errors compound.

source: Xia et al. (2024) Agentless: Demystifying LLM-based Software Engineering Agents
finding: A fixed three-phase pipeline (localise, repair, validate) with no agent control matched or beat open agents on SWE-bench Lite.
numbers: 32.00% (96 fixes) at about $0.70 per issue on SWE-bench Lite.
limits: Lite benchmark only; later systems have moved on.
agent_relevance: Hypothesise a location first, patch once, then validate: the expert order in code, with the program controlling flow.

source: Tian et al. (2024) DebugBench: Evaluating Debugging Capability of LLMs (Findings ACL 2024)
finding: Benchmark of 4,253 instances over 4 major bug types and 18 minor types in C++, Java, Python. Models fall short of human debugging. Runtime feedback helps syntax and reference bugs but can disrupt logic bugs.
numbers: 4,253 instances; 2 commercial and 4 open models, zero-shot.
limits: Bugs were implanted by GPT-4, not natural; feedback effect described in words, no figure read.
agent_relevance: Feedback is not always good: for logic bugs, low-level traces can mislead. Add the abstract failing assertion, not the raw trace.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug (ICLR 2024)
finding: Self-Debugging (explain code and use execution results) improved accuracy and sample efficiency across code benchmarks.
numbers: Spider +2-3% overall and +9% on hardest level; TransCoder and MBPP up to +12%; matches or beats baselines that draw more than 10x candidates.
limits: Only the abstract was read closely. Gain relies on unit tests or execution results where available; on Spider (no tests) it is smaller.
agent_relevance: Contrasts with the Huang and Olausson results: self-debug works when real execution feedback is the signal.
